newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ariane rocket launches INTELSAT satellite.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches INTELSAT satellite.

text.p: Western Europe's 96th Ariane rocket put a communications satellite for the 141 member-nation INTELSAT organisation into orbit after a textbook launch from equatorial French Guiana late on Wednesday.

The Ariane 44P rocket equipped with four solid strap-on boosters lifted off at 8.45 p.m. local time French Guiana time (2345 GMT) from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
Reporters watching the launch on video screens at the corporate headquarters of the Arianespace company near Paris saw the rocket lift off into a cloudy equatorial night sky.
Twenty minutes later, space officials said the INTELSAT 802 satellite separated from the Ariane rocket.

The Washington-based International Telecommuncations Satellite organisation (INTELSAT) said INTELSAT 802 is the second of the INTELSAT-8 series -- a run of six satellites with more capacity than the previous INTELSAT-7 family. The satellite will service the Indian Ocean region.
"The mission of INTELSAT-8 is a classic mission for INTELSAT: telephony, data transmission and televsion," Claude Burgio, INTELSAT vice president for engineering told Reuters.
"It's going to cover Asia, Australia and the Western United States. It will increase our global coverage and double our coverage in these areas," he said.
Burgio said the cost of INTELSAT 802 -- satellite, launch and insurance -- was in excess of $200 million.

INTELSAT, with 141 member nations, owns and operates 25 satellites and remains the world's largest operator of international satellites despite recent competition from private non-governmental providers. The organisation said 1996 revenues exceeded $911 million.

The 3.4 tonne satellite was built by U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin Telecommunications in New Jersey. It will have the capacity to provide up to 112,500 two-way telephone circuits using digital multiplication equipment and four television channels.
INTELSAT'S first satellite, Early Bird launched in 1965, was the world's first commercial telecommunications satellite. It carried 360 telephone circuits.

The Paris-based Arianespace company, which launches the Ariane-4 rocket series, has led the commercial satellite launch market since the late 1980's. Arch rival, International Launch Services (ILS), that launches the Atlas rocket series and Russia's Proton rocket, now says it has equalled Ariane's market share.
Arianespace has successfully placed 22 satellites aboard 14 Ariane-4 rockets since January 1996. The company says it now has firm orders to launch 43 heavy satellites worth an estimated $3.4 billion.
But in June 1996, the first more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in a major setback for the European space program.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over operations of Ariane-5 early this year, but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is planned for late September at earliest.
